Summary: Customer-experience reviewer for UI changes, workflow clarity, and accessibility-sensitive outcomes.
Purpose: Protect the usability, consistency, and accessibility quality of customer-facing interaction changes.
StaffingIntent: A senior design or UX reviewer with enough product context to challenge harmful interaction decisions.
SnapshotSummary: Customer-experience reviewer for UI changes, workflow clarity, and accessibility-sensitive outcomes.
SeniorityBand: Senior product design or UX leadership
KnowledgeRequirements: Ability to evaluate workflow clarity, accessibility, information hierarchy, and user-task completion risk.
Knowledge of established design-system conventions and when deviation is justified.
Understanding of how rushed UI change can create support or adoption cost despite technical correctness.
Ability to review evidence such as mockups, screenshots, prototypes, and implementation diffs.
Knowledge of accessibility obligations relevant to the product surface.
Ability to convert subjective UX concerns into actionable review findings.
ExperienceRequirements: Has reviewed or designed customer-facing software workflows in production contexts.
Has caught usability or accessibility issues before release and driven correction.
Has collaborated with engineers to preserve design intent within implementation constraints.
Has used qualitative or support-driven feedback to improve shipped flows.
Has balanced UX quality with release timing in a documented decision.
DecisionRights: Approve or reject UX-sensitive change progression when designated.
Require accessibility or usability validation before release on impacted surfaces.
Escalate when design-system or accessibility debt is being knowingly increased.
Demand customer-facing evidence when workflow change risk is material.
CollaborationExpectations: Collaborate with product, engineering, and QA on impacted user flows.
Provide specific review guidance instead of taste-based criticism.
Join release decisions when UI risk materially affects adoption or support.
Capture recurring UX issues for follow-up improvement.
AntiPatterns: Treating subjective preference as a release blocker without risk framing.
Reviewing too late to influence the outcome constructively.
Ignoring accessibility because the change is visually small.
Approving UX-sensitive changes without seeing evidence of the actual implemented flow.
FitnessEvidence: Review artifacts with traceable UX decisions.
Examples of usability or accessibility issues prevented before release.
Alignment from engineering that the role’s feedback is actionable.
Evidence of improved customer-facing workflow quality.
